pathway.title: Magnera Corp — Credit Snapshot
pathway.question: Should we own this issuer, in which instrument, and why?

runs.text: First, leverage is improving on filed figures but is sensitive to the earnings definition. Magnera's gross debt was USD 1,966 million at June 27, 2026 against LTM adjusted EBITDA of USD 372 million, giving 5.28x gross and 4.53x net, down from 5.74x and 4.88x at September 27, 2025 (Documentary Fact; basis CP-1 Chart data: leverage). The reduction came from higher LTM adjusted EBITDA and USD 65 million of repayments, with earnings contributing somewhat more. Operating income plus depreciation and amortization was USD 250 million LTM, so leverage would be 7.86x gross on that basis; add-backs of USD 122 million are about one third of adjusted EBITDA (Analyst Interpretation; CP-1 Financials and credit metrics). The mechanism is that every quarter carries restructuring and integration add-backs, so creditors should treat the adjusted figure as the issuer's own measure and rely on the unadjusted figure for downside testing.

Second, coverage is adequate only on the adjusted measure. Magnera's LTM adjusted EBITDA covers a cash-interest proxy 2.91x, but LTM operating income of USD 63 million covers net interest expense of USD 151 million only 0.42x, and the issuer reported a net loss in every period shown, USD 112 million LTM (Documentary Fact and calculation; CP-1 Chart data: interest cover). The cash-interest figure for interim periods is a proxy, not a reported amount. The implication is that interest is paid from depreciation and non-cash charges rather than from operating profit, so any EBITDA shortfall reaches liquidity quickly.

Third, cash conversion is the weak link in the near term. Magnera generated USD 32 million of free cash flow in nine months of fiscal 2026 and a negative USD 28 million in the third quarter, as working capital absorbed USD 54 million (calculated by difference in CP-1). Management guides to USD 90 million to USD 110 million for the year, which requires USD 58 million to USD 78 million in the fourth quarter (Management Language for the guidance; Analyst Interpretation for the requirement). Raw-material inventory rose in the third quarter and the price-cost spread helped earnings, so cash and margin both depend on how fast cost changes pass through (CP-1A Company and operating model, Pricing and pass-through). The implication is that deleveraging pace in the next two quarters is a function of working capital release, not of earnings growth.

Fourth, liquidity and maturities favour creditors, with one unverified element. Magnera had USD 280 million of cash, about 58% of it outside the U.S., plus a USD 350 million asset-based revolver commitment with no borrowings, a combined USD 630 million before any borrowing base or letters of credit (Documentary Fact; CP-1 Chart data: liquidity). The revolver's availability, drawn letters of credit and covenants are Not supplied (Insufficient Information). The term loan and the notes carry no financial maintenance covenant, which lowers the chance of a covenant-driven default (Documentary Fact; CP-1 Instruments, liquidity build and covenants). The implication is that near-term default risk is low on the information supplied, and the question moves to refinancing.

Fifth, refinancing risk is concentrated. The 4.75% notes of USD 500 million mature in October 2029, the revolver in November 2029, and the term loan of USD 706 million and 7.25% notes of USD 760 million in November 2031 (CP-1 Chart data: debt maturities). A quarter of debt falls due in 2029 and three quarters in 2031 (calc). Management says it intends to refinance prior to maturity, and the fair value of the debt sat USD 48 million below book at June 27, 2026 against USD 136 million at March 28, 2026 (CP-1 Interpretation). The mechanism is that a weak operating year in fiscal 2027 or 2028 would meet the 2029 maturity wall with leverage still above five times gross, narrowing refinancing options; the implication is a monitoring posture focused on deleveraging progress and market access ahead of 2028.

Sixth, the business gives limited revenue visibility. The top ten customers were about 42% of FY2025 net sales, the largest about 14%, and many customers have no long-term arrangements (Documentary Fact; CP-1A Company and operating model, Customers and Contract tenor). Organic volume fell 1% in nine months while currency and the merger lifted reported sales (CP-1A Volume and price drivers). The implication is that revenue can move quickly with account decisions, so creditors rely on cost pass-through and the Americas segment, which earns about two thirds of adjusted EBITDA, rather than on contracted revenue.

Seventh, reporting reliability and related-party dependence are open items. Material weaknesses and ineffective disclosure controls persist at June 27, 2026, and legacy IT still runs under a transition services agreement with the former parent (Documentary Fact; CP-1A Ownership and issuer-level governance behaviour). The implication is that interim figures carry control risk and that remediation status at the fiscal 2026 annual report is a monitoring trigger; the terms of the agreement are Not supplied.

runs.text: Strengths. A long maturity runway is the first strength: Magnera has no debt maturing before October 2029, and its term loan and notes carry no financial maintenance covenant (Documentary Fact; CP-1 Chart data: debt maturities and covenants). Liquidity is the second: USD 280 million of cash and a USD 350 million undrawn revolver commitment total USD 630 million, with no facility expiring within twelve months (Documentary Fact; CP-1 Chart data: liquidity), though availability is unconfirmed. Deleveraging behaviour is the third: gross leverage fell from 5.74x to 5.28x, USD 65 million of debt was repaid in nine months and the equity statements show no dividends or buybacks (Documentary Fact; CP-1 Chart data: leverage and CP-1A Ownership and issuer-level governance behaviour). Rate exposure is the fourth: USD 1,260 million, about 64%, of debt is fixed-rate notes, and the filing puts a quarter-point move in floating rates at about USD 2 million of annual interest (Analyst Interpretation, calculated from the debt table; CP-1 Instruments). Operating scale and diversity are the fifth: 45 manufacturing facilities across two segments and consumer-oriented end markets, with the Americas earning a higher margin (Documentary Fact and Management Language for the stability description; CP-1A Company and operating model).

Weaknesses. Earnings quality is the first weakness: add-backs of USD 122 million LTM, recurring restructuring and integration charges, and unadjusted leverage of 7.86x gross (Analyst Interpretation; CP-1 Financials and credit metrics). Interest burden is the second: net interest expense of USD 151 million LTM against operating income of USD 63 million and a net loss every period (Documentary Fact and calculation; CP-1). Cash flow is the third: free cash flow of USD 32 million for nine months against guidance requiring a strong fourth quarter, and unquantified receivable programmes that sit outside reported debt (Documentary Fact; CP-1 Claims outside the debt figure). Customer concentration and short contract tenor are the fourth (Documentary Fact; CP-1A). Reporting controls and dependence on the former parent's systems are the fifth (Documentary Fact; CP-1A). Claims outside debt are the sixth: operating leases of USD 60 million, a cross-currency swap liability of USD 78 million, Brazilian tax claims of up to USD 66 million, an environmental liability of USD 17 million against a USD 9 million escrow asset and an unfunded pension obligation of USD 27 million at September 27, 2025 (Documentary Fact; CP-1 Claims outside the debt figure; treating all as debt would lift gross leverage to about 5.95x, calc). Equity quality is the seventh: book equity of USD 1,017 million is mostly goodwill and intangibles of USD 858 million, leaving tangible equity of about USD 159 million (Analyst Interpretation, calculated from the balance sheet in CP-1).

runs.text: The transaction that created the issuer closed on November 4, 2024: Treasure Holdco, Inc., a wholly owned subsidiary of Berry Global Group, Inc., merged with Glatfelter Corporation, which concurrently changed its name to Magnera Corporation [10-K_2025-09-27 page:5] "completed its merger (the “Transaction”) with the Glatfelter Corporation". The agreement is listed in the exhibit index as an RMT transaction agreement dated February 6, 2024 [10-K_2025-09-27 page:45] "2.1† RMT Transaction Agreement" (the agreement itself is not supplied; the label is the issuer's). Pre-transaction Treasure shareholders received shares representing 90 percent of the combined company and Glatfelter shareholders retained 10 percent [10-K_2025-09-27 page:5] "pre-Transaction Treasure shareholders received shares of Magnera representing 90% of the combined company". Treasure was the accounting acquirer, so pre-closing history is the carve-out of the former parent's business and the Glatfelter business is consolidated from the closing date. The purchase consideration for the Glatfelter equity was recorded at 74, with goodwill of 36 on the transaction [10-K_2025-09-27 page:32] "Fair value of GLT common stock concurrent with closing $ 74" and "Goodwill 36", and Glatfelter debt of 869 was assumed in the allocation [10-K_2025-09-27 page:32] "Debt (869 )". The Glatfelter contribution to FY2025 net sales was 1,145 [10-K_2025-09-27 page:32] "The net sales for the year ended September 27, 2025 included $1,145 million from GLT." and unaudited pro forma FY2025 net sales and net loss including Glatfelter for the full year were 3,316 and (165) [10-K_2025-09-27 page:32] "unaudited pro forma net sales and net loss were $3,316 million and $(165) million".

New debt raised at closing. The issuer consummated a 785 term loan due 2031, an 800 issuance of 7.25% first priority senior secured notes due 2031 and a 350 revolving credit facility [10-K_2025-09-27 page:34] "As part of the Transaction, the Company consummated a $785 million Term Loan due 2031". Use of proceeds: "The proceeds from the Term Loan and 7.25% Notes were used to retire a portion of GLT outstanding debt and fund a cash distribution to Berry." [10-K_2025-09-27 page:34]. The distribution to Berry was 1,111 [10-K_2025-09-27 page:25] "Cash distribution to Berry (1,111 ) — —", against proceeds from long-term borrowings of 1,556 in the cash flow statement, which is 29 below the 1,585 face amount of the term loan and notes (calc); the supplied text does not explain the 29. Berry also transferred its health, hygiene and specialties global nonwovens and films business to Treasure as part of the closing [10-K_2025-09-27 page:26] "Berry received a cash distribution and, in turn, transferred". A prepayment penalty of 15 was charged for retiring debt concurrently with the transaction [10-K_2025-09-27 page:16] "a $15 million prepayment penalty charge for retiring debt concurrently with the Transaction". The retained Glatfelter 4.75% first priority senior secured notes due October 2029 remain outstanding at 500 [10-K_2025-09-27 page:34] "retained GLT 4.75 % First Priority Senior Secured Notes"; the indentures and a first supplemental indenture are exhibits but not supplied, so issuer and co-issuer entities, guarantors and collateral are not documented here beyond the names in the exhibit index [10-K_2025-09-27 page:46] "4.1 Indenture, by and between Treasure Escrow Corporation".

Liquidity and status. The transaction brought cash of 37 into the group (acquired cash), and cash was 305 at September 27, 2025 and 280 at June 27, 2026 (CP-1). The transaction is complete; the 10-K presents the final allocation [10-K_2025-09-27 page:32] "The following table summarizes the final purchase price allocation:" and describes the measurement period adjustments. There was no new debt issuance in the first nine months of FY2026; the only financing flows are repayments of 65. Subsequent events: no new issuance or refinancing is reported in any supplied source dated after the closing, and nothing is supplied after August 6, 2026. Management says it intends to refinance long-term debt prior to maturity [10-Q_2026-06-27 page:19] "which we intend to refinance prior to maturity"; no refinancing is documented. Management's pro forma adjusted EBITDA includes a synergy add-on that fell across the three releases: [EX-99.1_2026-02-05 page:6] "Synergies and cost reductions 60", [EX-99.1_2026-05-07 page:6] "Synergies and cost reductions 48" and [EX-99.1_2026-08-06 page:6] "Synergies and cost reductions 35". These are attributed management figures, not filed results. The pro forma total moved from 423 to 412 to 405 [EX-99.1_2026-02-05 page:6] "Comparable Adjusted EBITDA (1)(6) $ 423", [EX-99.1_2026-05-07 page:6] "PF Adjusted EBITDA $ 412" and [EX-99.1_2026-08-06 page:6] "PF Adjusted EBITDA $ 405", while the filed LTM adjusted EBITDA built in CP-1 rose from 363 to 364 to 372; the direction of the two series differs because the synergy add-on shrank faster than LTM earnings grew. Whether the shrinking add-on reflects realisation of synergies in reported results is Analyst Interpretation and is not stated by the issuer.

fields.value: Debt capacity evidence. The latest debt note lists four instruments and a footing total, and states that the term loan and secured notes carry no financial maintenance covenants: [10-Q_2026-06-27 page:9] "Despite not having financial maintenance covenants on our term loan and secured notes". The source risk is that the revolver is described separately as an asset-based facility with no borrowings, yet its covenant, availability and letter of credit terms are not printed anywhere in the pack. The consequence is that downstream liquidity can use cash and the stated revolver size but must present undrawn capacity as unconfirmed, and must not state that no covenant applies to the revolver. The compliance statement covers "all long-term debt covenants": [10-Q_2026-06-27 page:9] "We are in compliance with all long-term debt covenants as of June 27, 2026."

fields.value: Refinancing evidence. Management says it intends to refinance, and the annual report states there are no maturities before 2029: [10-K_2025-09-27 page:34] "The Company has no future maturities of long-term debt until 2029, at which point $500 million and $1,531 million are due in fiscal year 2029 and 2031, respectively". Source risk: the maturity schedule is printed only in the annual report and as of September 27, 2025; interim notes give maturity dates but no schedule, and no source after August 6, 2026 can show a refinancing. Consequence: the maturity wall for the cutoff must be rebuilt from the interim debt table and labelled as derived, and any refinancing between August 6, 2026 and the cutoff is unknown.

fields.value: Leverage. Evidence: gross debt principal fell from 2,031 at September 27, 2025 to 1,966 at June 27, 2026 through repayments of the term loan (731 to 706) and the 7.25% notes (800 to 760) [10-Q_2026-06-27 page:8] "7.25% First Priority Senior Secured Notes November 2031 760 800", while LTM adjusted EBITDA rose from 354 to 372. Risk mechanism: both legs help, but the EBITDA is a company-defined measure and the gap to operating income plus D&A is 122 LTM. Credit implication: filed-basis leverage of 5.28x gross and 4.53x net is improving but remains above five times gross for a business that reports a net loss in every period shown. Higher LTM EBITDA contributed somewhat more of the improvement than debt repayment (calc: EBITDA change alone gives 5.46, debt change alone 5.55; see Calculations).

fields.value: Add-backs and definition risk. Evidence: segment notes reconcile adjusted EBITDA to operating income through restructuring and integration charges, Argentina hyperinflation, carve-out allocation and other non-cash charges; the LTM restructuring and other activities charge was 81, and the nine-month charge of 61 splits into severance 13, facility exit 3, non-cash 10 and integration and other 35 [10-Q_2026-06-27 page:7] "Charges 13 3 10 35 61". The 10-K sized only the Project CORE capacity rationalisation at about 20 over two years [10-K_2025-09-27 page:15] "these actions are projected to cost approximately $20 million"; the charge line is therefore broader than that programme, and the integration and other component recurs each quarter, with a further 23 in Q3 including a loss on sale of a facility. Risk mechanism: add-backs that recur every quarter blur the line between non-recurring and operating cost; lenders and rating methodologies may haircut them. Credit implication: committee leverage should be shown on both bases (5.28x and 7.86x gross), and a covenant-style EBITDA cannot be inferred because no definition from an executed agreement is supplied.

fields.value: The supplied sources show a mid-sized, publicly listed manufacturer of nonwoven and film-based specialty materials for consumer-oriented end markets, formed in a combination in which a carve-out of the former parent's health, hygiene and specialties business merged with Glatfelter. The structure matters to a creditor in three ways. First, the combination was financed with new first priority secured debt and a cash distribution to the former parent, so opening leverage was set by the transaction rather than by operations; since closing the documented capital allocation is voluntary debt repayment, with no dividends or buybacks in the equity statements. Second, the integration is incomplete: the issuer reports material weaknesses tied to the merger and still depends on the former parent's legacy IT systems under a transition services agreement, so the reporting base is exposed to a counterparty that is also the former owner. Third, the operating model combines high input-cost pass-through with lag, a large customer concentration (top ten about 42 percent of FY2025 net sales) and a geographic mix in which Rest of World, the lower-margin segment, is the largest region in the nine-month geographic table. No sponsor, controlling holder or related-party financing is documented in the supplied text; that is a gap in the evidence, not a finding of absence. The view is bounded by what is not supplied: the merger agreements, the proxy statement, the indentures and credit agreements, and any source dated after August 6, 2026.

fields.value: 1. Revenue durability. Evidence: no long-term arrangements with many customers [10-K_2025-09-27 page:8] "since we do not have long-term arrangements with many of our customers" and a top-ten share of about 42 percent [10-K_2025-09-27 page:27] "our top ten customers represented approximately 42% of net sales". Credit implication: debt service cannot lean on contracted revenue, so leverage tolerance should be lower than for contract-backed businesses, and monitoring should watch organic volume (negative at nine months) and any top-account loss. fields.value: 2. Margin and cash-flow risk. Evidence: input costs are polymer resin and pulps passed on with lag; a favourable price-cost spread of 11 in Q3 helped, while selling prices fell by 117 at nine months. Risk mechanic: in rising-cost periods the lag compresses margin and absorbs working capital (raw-material inventory rose in Q3, CP-1 shows free cash flow of (28) in Q3). Credit implication: cash conversion is the weak link in the near term; fourth-quarter delivery of the free cash flow guidance range is the monitoring point. Counter: management reports that Project CORE and synergy benefits are being realised [EX-99.1_2026-08-06 page:2] "realized benefits from Project CORE and merger synergies".

fields.name: Quote

Evidence: Rest of World is about 45 percent of nine-month net sales, 58 percent of cash is outside the U.S. (CP-1) and unremitted foreign earnings were 336 at fiscal 2025 year end [10-K_2025-09-27 page:18] "Our unremitted foreign earnings were $336 million at the end of fiscal 2025." Risk mechanic: dollar debt is serviced from cash flows generated partly in euro, sterling and Brazilian real; repatriation is described by management as without significant restriction but the tax cost is not estimated. Credit implication: net debt that nets all cash overstates readily available liquidity at the U.S. borrower level, and translation moves reported leverage. Counter: the euro cross-currency swaps hedge part of the net investment.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: 4. Transaction and integration risk. Evidence: material weaknesses tied to the merger, reliance on legacy Berry IT under a transition services agreement, restructuring and integration charges recurring each quarter (CP-1). Risk mechanic: integration is incomplete and a former parent provides services; a failure of control or service continuity could delay reporting or disrupt order-to-cash. Credit implication: reporting reliability is a standing limitation and the monitoring posture should include remediation status at the FY2026 annual report. Counter: the auditor's opinion on the FY2025 financial statements was unqualified and management states there were no material errors.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Magnera's creditors hold a leveraged but adequately liquid credit that is improving slowly and is not yet proven. Its strongest support is a long runway: the debt stack of USD 1,966 million has no maturity before October 2029, cash is USD 280 million, a USD 350 million revolver commitment is undrawn, and the issuer repaid USD 65 million in nine months without distributions. Its weakest point is the quality of the earnings and cash flow behind a 5.28x gross leverage figure: add-backs are USD 122 million of USD 372 million LTM adjusted EBITDA, operating income covers net interest only 0.42x, nine-month free cash flow was USD 32 million, and reporting controls are ineffective. The outcome turns on fourth-quarter cash delivery, on refinancing USD 500 million in 2029 and USD 1,466 million in 2031, and on revolver and covenant terms that are not yet visible.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: First, leverage is improving on filed figures but is sensitive to the earnings definition. Magnera's gross debt was USD 1,966 million at June 27, 2026 against LTM adjusted EBITDA of USD 372 million, giving 5.28x gross and 4.53x net, down from 5.74x and 4.88x at September 27, 2025 (Documentary Fact; basis CP-1 Chart data: leverage). The reduction came from higher LTM adjusted EBITDA and USD 65 million of repayments, with earnings contributing somewhat more. Operating income plus depreciation and amortization was USD 250 million LTM, so leverage would be 7.86x gross on that basis; add-backs of USD 122 million are about one third of adjusted EBITDA (Analyst Interpretation; CP-1 Financials and credit metrics). The mechanism is that every quarter carries restructuring and integration add-backs, so creditors should treat the adjusted figure as the issuer's own measure and rely on the unadjusted figure for downside testing.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Second, coverage is adequate only on the adjusted measure. Magnera's LTM adjusted EBITDA covers a cash-interest proxy 2.91x, but LTM operating income of USD 63 million covers net interest expense of USD 151 million only 0.42x, and the issuer reported a net loss in every period shown, USD 112 million LTM (Documentary Fact and calculation; CP-1 Chart data: interest cover). The cash-interest figure for interim periods is a proxy, not a reported amount. The implication is that interest is paid from depreciation and non-cash charges rather than from operating profit, so any EBITDA shortfall reaches liquidity quickly.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Third, cash conversion is the weak link in the near term. Magnera generated USD 32 million of free cash flow in nine months of fiscal 2026 and a negative USD 28 million in the third quarter, as working capital absorbed USD 54 million (calculated by difference in CP-1). Management guides to USD 90 million to USD 110 million for the year, which requires USD 58 million to USD 78 million in the fourth quarter (Management Language for the guidance; Analyst Interpretation for the requirement). Raw-material inventory rose in the third quarter and the price-cost spread helped earnings, so cash and margin both depend on how fast cost changes pass through (CP-1A Company and operating model, Pricing and pass-through). The implication is that deleveraging pace in the next two quarters is a function of working capital release, not of earnings growth.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Fourth, liquidity and maturities favour creditors, with one unverified element. Magnera had USD 280 million of cash, about 58% of it outside the U.S., plus a USD 350 million asset-based revolver commitment with no borrowings, a combined USD 630 million before any borrowing base or letters of credit (Documentary Fact; CP-1 Chart data: liquidity). The revolver's availability, drawn letters of credit and covenants are Not supplied (Insufficient Information). The term loan and the notes carry no financial maintenance covenant, which lowers the chance of a covenant-driven default (Documentary Fact; CP-1 Instruments, liquidity build and covenants). The implication is that near-term default risk is low on the information supplied, and the question moves to refinancing.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Fifth, refinancing risk is concentrated. The 4.75% notes of USD 500 million mature in October 2029, the revolver in November 2029, and the term loan of USD 706 million and 7.25% notes of USD 760 million in November 2031 (CP-1 Chart data: debt maturities). A quarter of debt falls due in 2029 and three quarters in 2031 (calc). Management says it intends to refinance prior to maturity, and the fair value of the debt sat USD 48 million below book at June 27, 2026 against USD 136 million at March 28, 2026 (CP-1 Interpretation). The mechanism is that a weak operating year in fiscal 2027 or 2028 would meet the 2029 maturity wall with leverage still above five times gross, narrowing refinancing options; the implication is a monitoring posture focused on deleveraging progress and market access ahead of 2028.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Sixth, the business gives limited revenue visibility. The top ten customers were about 42% of FY2025 net sales, the largest about 14%, and many customers have no long-term arrangements (Documentary Fact; CP-1A Company and operating model, Customers and Contract tenor). Organic volume fell 1% in nine months while currency and the merger lifted reported sales (CP-1A Volume and price drivers). The implication is that revenue can move quickly with account decisions, so creditors rely on cost pass-through and the Americas segment, which earns about two thirds of adjusted EBITDA, rather than on contracted revenue.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Seventh, reporting reliability and related-party dependence are open items. Material weaknesses and ineffective disclosure controls persist at June 27, 2026, and legacy IT still runs under a transition services agreement with the former parent (Documentary Fact; CP-1A Ownership and issuer-level governance behaviour). The implication is that interim figures carry control risk and that remediation status at the fiscal 2026 annual report is a monitoring trigger; the terms of the agreement are Not supplied.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Strengths. A long maturity runway is the first strength: Magnera has no debt maturing before October 2029, and its term loan and notes carry no financial maintenance covenant (Documentary Fact; CP-1 Chart data: debt maturities and covenants). Liquidity is the second: USD 280 million of cash and a USD 350 million undrawn revolver commitment total USD 630 million, with no facility expiring within twelve months (Documentary Fact; CP-1 Chart data: liquidity), though availability is unconfirmed. Deleveraging behaviour is the third: gross leverage fell from 5.74x to 5.28x, USD 65 million of debt was repaid in nine months and the equity statements show no dividends or buybacks (Documentary Fact; CP-1 Chart data: leverage and CP-1A Ownership and issuer-level governance behaviour). Rate exposure is the fourth: USD 1,260 million, about 64%, of debt is fixed-rate notes, and the filing puts a quarter-point move in floating rates at about USD 2 million of annual interest (Analyst Interpretation, calculated from the debt table; CP-1 Instruments). Operating scale and diversity are the fifth: 45 manufacturing facilities across two segments and consumer-oriented end markets, with the Americas earning a higher margin (Documentary Fact and Management Language for the stability description; CP-1A Company and operating model).

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Weaknesses. Earnings quality is the first weakness: add-backs of USD 122 million LTM, recurring restructuring and integration charges, and unadjusted leverage of 7.86x gross (Analyst Interpretation; CP-1 Financials and credit metrics). Interest burden is the second: net interest expense of USD 151 million LTM against operating income of USD 63 million and a net loss every period (Documentary Fact and calculation; CP-1).
